Work  /  Standard & Poor’s DRI
Direct mail · Print production · Campaign design

How do you mail someone a forecast?

Standard & Poor’s DRI sold economic data — price and wage projections across 400 industries and 175 countries. There was nothing to photograph and nothing to hold. Three campaigns made the product physical.

Client

Standard & Poor’s DRI · DRI-WEFA

Services

Campaign design, dielines, print management

Sector

Economic data & forecasting

Recognition

Monadnock Paper Award, 2002

Show Me The Money. The folder opens to pockets holding sample reports, a case study, and a fax-back form.

The challenge

A subscription to numbers is a hard thing to sell through the mail. The buyer was a purchasing manager or a construction executive who had never heard of DRI, had no reason to open the envelope, and could not be shown the product because the product was a spreadsheet.

This was 2002. There was no demo to click, no video to autoplay, no trial to start. Whatever the mail piece did in the first three seconds on a desk was the entire pitch.

The approach

Make the abstract physical. Each campaign turned the offer into an object the recipient had to do something with — open a box, assemble a puzzle, unfold a mailer, keep a notepad on the desk. The engagement was the argument: if you will spend thirty seconds putting this together, you will spend thirty seconds understanding what we sell.

The headlines followed the same rule. Not comprehensive econometric modeling. Power tools for purchasers. Get the whole picture. Show me the money.

The mechanical. Folder and insert dielines, notepad position, letter inserts — one file carrying the whole assembly.

Show Me The Money

A pocket folder built around a promise of utility rather than insight. The cover carries four words and a logo. Inside, the panels do the selling in sequence: information is power, then rely on the experts, then see for yourself with a free issue and a phone number.

The credibility sits in a single column of small red type on the red panel — Boeing, Daimler-Chrysler, Motorola, Lockheed-Martin, Exxon, American Airlines, the State of California. No claims about it. Just the list.

This campaign won the Monadnock Paper Award in 2002.

Global Industry Insight. A cube that opens to a jigsaw with one piece loose.

Global Industry Insight

Get the whole picture — delivered as a puzzle with a piece missing. The line and the object say the same thing, so neither has to explain the other. The cube gives the mailer weight on a desk and a reason to be opened; the folded brochure inside carries the detail for anyone who wants it.

Global Construction Study 2002. A self-mailer with the reply card built into the fold.
One offer, three entry points — the same campaign sized for different placements.

Global Construction Study

Produced under the DRI-WEFA mark in the summer of 2002, while the business itself was being sold, merged and renamed around the work. A mosaic of small photographs builds into a grid on the cover — fragments resolving into a picture, which is what a forecast is.

The reply card folds into the mailer, so responding costs the reader nothing but a pen.

The outcome

Show Me The Money won the Monadnock Paper Award in 2002 — an award judged on paper, print and production, which is the right frame for work whose whole argument was that it existed as an object.

Every piece here was die-cut, folded, pocketed or perforated. The design and the dielines came from the same desk, which is the only reason the assembly worked at the bindery.
